idiom_name: lambda x: x plus the key=None convention
implementation_notes: Python has no stdlib identity function: the operator module exposes C-implemented operator equivalents and object-identity tests (is_/is_not) but deliberately no single-argument identity (a 2025 proposal to add operator.identity, cpython issue 132341, stalled on the objection that it is an attractive nuisance), so the canonical realization is a local lambda x: x or, where type hints or reuse matter, a named def identity(x: T) -> T. What replaces the classic structure is twofold: the stdlib key=None convention - sorted, min, max, heapq.merge and itertools.groupby all interpret a None key as 'use the element itself', so callers omit the key instead of passing an identity - and functools.reduce, whose explicit initializer argument is where the neutral element of a fold lives. The explicit form is still justified when a reusable API must accept a Callable[[T], T] slot that is populated unconditionally (optional pipeline stages, composable middleware, typed code where lambda carries no annotations): defining one shared, annotated identity beats scattering anonymous lambdas. Note that CPython neither inlines the lambda away nor elides the call - each use is a real frame push, which is why the operator module exists for the operators it does cover.
code_sketch:
from functools import reduce
from typing import Callable, TypeVar
T = TypeVar('T')
def identity(x: T) -> T: return x          # the canonical form
# composition fold: identity is the neutral element of the empty pipeline
def compose(fns: list[Callable[[T], T]]) -> Callable[[T], T]:
    return reduce(lambda acc, f: lambda x: f(acc(x)), fns, identity)
# consumer-side convention: key=None already means identity
best = max(items, key=None)                # not max(items, key=identity)
pitfalls: Builtin name collision: id(x) is the object-identity builtin returning the memory address as an int, not the value; writing id where the identity function was meant type-checks dynamically and silently produces a wrong number.

lambda x: x carries no annotations, so type checkers see no Callable[[T], T] binding and downstream inference degrades to untyped; assign it to an annotated variable or use a typed def when a generic slot must stay checked.

Arity mismatches surface only at runtime: reduce(lambda x: x, xs) fails on the first pair because reduce calls its function with two arguments, and a unary identity passed where a key function's contract differs fails equally late - there is no compile-time catch.

CPython does not inline lambda x: x away: in a tight loop each call is a Python-level frame push, so hoist the function out of the loop and measure before inserting identity into latency-critical paths.

Identity preserves the reference, not a snapshot: map(identity, xs) yields the same mutable objects, so later in-place mutations are visible through the 'untransformed' result and downstream code cannot distinguish a real transformation from a pass-through when logging only outputs.

Do not conflate the key=None convention with the map/filter function slot: map(None, xs) was Python 2 only and raises TypeError in Python 3 - None means identity only where the API documents it (sorted/min/max/groupby key parameters).
